summary: To weep: to shed tears and cry aloud, the voice lifted up in grief, at the meeting and parting of kin, for the dead, in complaint, and before Yahweh in entreaty and repentance. The qal is weep or bewail (with an object, עַל or לְ: weep for); the piel, twice, is the lament of mourners, Rachel for her sons and the women for the Tammuz; the nouns בְּכִי, בֶּכֶה, בְּכִית and בָּכוּת are weeping and the days of mourning for the dead. Its opposite is laughter and the ringing shout of joy (Ecc 3:4; Psa 30:6), and the prophets promise a Jerusalem where the voice of weeping is heard no more (Isa 65:19). The verb is the same in Arabic, Akkadian, Ugaritic, Ge'ez and Aramaic, the Peshitta's word for the weeping of the Gospels.

words.summary: About 115 times, almost all qal. Weeping is with the voice and with tears: the voice is “lifted up” and the eyes run with water (Gen 21:16; Lam 1:16; Jer 8:23), and Yahweh sees the tears (2Ki 20:5). Its usual companions are fasting, mourning (סָפַד, אָבַל) and tears (דִּמְעָה); its opposites laughter and the shout of joy. The brief's ten verb tokens with no stem are the noun בְּכִי and the place name Bochim, filed here by spelling.

senses.definition: To shed tears and cry aloud, from grief, distress or strong feeling: often “lift up the voice and weep”, of a mother, an infant, a king, an army, or kin meeting again after long parting and falling on each other's neck. Figuratively the furrows of a wronged field weep (Job 31:38).

evidence.note: Hagar, not to see the child die, “lifted up her voice וַתֵּבְךְּ”.
“Hannah, why do you weep (תִבְכִּי), and why do you not eat, and why is your heart grieved?”
David and the people “lifted up their voice and wept, until there was no strength in them לִבְכּוֹת”.
“For these things I weep (בוֹכִיָּה); my eye, my eye runs down with water.”
“A time לִבְכּוֹת and a time to laugh (לִשְׂחוֹק).”
Pharaoh's daughter opened the ark, “and behold, a boy weeping (בֹּכֶה)”.
“Jacob kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice and wept.”
Esau fell on Jacob's neck and kissed him, “and they wept”.
Joseph's compassion was stirred for his brother; “he sought where to weep, and went into the chamber and wept there”.
Joseph fell on Benjamin's neck “וַיֵּבְךְּ, and Benjamin wept on his neck”.
Esau, the blessing gone: “Bless me, me also, my father! And Esau lifted up his voice and wept.”
David and Jonathan at parting “kissed one another and wept one with another”.
Naomi's daughters-in-law at parting.
Job's friends did not know him, “and lifted up their voice and wept”.
David went up the ascent of the olives “weeping as he went up”, his head covered.
At the news from Jabesh “all the people lifted up their voices and wept”.
“He goes on his way weeping (וּבָכֹה), bearing the seed to sow; he shall come again with a ringing shout (בְרִנָּה), bearing his sheaves.”
The old men who had seen the first house “wept (בֹּכִים) with a loud voice”, while many shouted for joy.
Esther “fell at his feet and wept” to plead for her people.
Ishmael came out to meet the men “weeping as he went”, a feigned weeping before the murder.
“The messengers of peace weep bitterly (מַר יִבְכָּיוּן).”
“Awake, drunkards, and weep, and wail, all drinkers of wine.”
“My pipe to the voice of those who weep (בֹּכִים).”
“If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep together (יִבְכָּיוּן).”
“My soul shall weep in secret for your pride.”
“A people shall dwell in Zion at Jerusalem; בָּכוֹ לֹא־תִבְכֶּה: you shall weep no more.”
“Tell it not in Gath; weep not at all (בָּכוֹ אַל־תִּבְכּוּ).”
“Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep”: the Peshitta's בְּכָא.

senses.definition: With an object, עַל, אֶל or לְ: to weep for the dead, or for one lost or a ruin coming, often for a set time and together with mourning (סָפַד, אָבַל) and fasting.

evidence.note: Sarah died, and Abraham came “to mourn for Sarah וְלִבְכֹּתָהּ”.
“The Egyptians wept for him (וַיִּבְכּוּ אֹתוֹ) seventy days.”
“The sons of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, and the days of weeping, the mourning for Moses, were ended.”
“They wept for Aaron thirty days, all the house of Israel.”
Jacob: “I will go down to my son mourning to the grave (שְׁאֹלָה). And his father wept for him.”
Joseph fell on his father's face, wept over him, and kissed him.
“They mourned (וַיִּסְפְּדוּ) and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan.”
“Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul.”
The king wept at Abner's grave, and all the people wept again over him.
“O my son Absalom … would I had died in your place!”; “the king weeps and mourns for Absalom”.

David fasted and wept while the child lived, “for I said, Who knows whether Yahweh will be gracious to me”; when it died he stopped: “Can I bring him back again? I go to him, but he will not return to me.”
The captive woman “shall weep for her father and her mother a month of days”.
“All the house of Israel shall bewail (יִבְכּוּ) the burning that Yahweh has kindled.”
Jephthah's daughter: “let me … weep over my virginity, I and my companions”.
“Do not weep for the dead (לְמֵת) nor bemoan him; weep bitterly (בְּכוּ בָכוֹ) for him who goes away, for he shall return no more nor see his native land.”
Ezekiel's wife taken: “you shall not mourn nor weep, nor shall your tears run down”; a sign to Israel (Ezk 24:23).
“His widows shall not weep.”
“Their widows made no lamentation.”
“O that my head were waters and my eye a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!”
Joash wept over the dying Elisha: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen!”
Elisha wept, “because I know the evil that you will do to the sons of Israel”.
“Therefore I will weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I will drench you with my tears.”
Over Tyre: “they shall weep for you in bitterness of soul with bitter mourning.”
“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yes, we wept, when we remembered Zion.”
“She weeps bitterly in the night (בָּכוֹ תִבְכֶּה בַּלַּיְלָה).”
“Did I not weep for him whose day was hard?”
“Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children”: weeping for a ruin to come, as Jer 22:10.

senses.gloss: weep before Yahweh, in entreaty or repentance
senses.definition: To weep in prayer, supplication or repentance, “before Yahweh” or at his house, often with fasting; a weeping Yahweh hears and answers.

evidence.note: Hannah, bitter of soul, “prayed to Yahweh וּבָכֹה תִבְכֶּה”.
Hezekiah prayed, “and Hezekiah wept a great weeping”; Yahweh answered, “I have heard your prayer, I have seen your tears” (2Ki 20:5).
Josiah: “because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before Yahweh … and tore your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard”.
Of Jacob at Peniel: “he strove with the messenger and prevailed; he wept (בָּכָה) and sought his favour.”
At the messenger's rebuke “the people lifted up their voice and wept”, and called the place Bochim, “weepers”.
At Bethel “they wept and sat there before Yahweh and fasted that day until evening”.
“They lifted up their voices and wept a great weeping.”
Ezra prayed and confessed, “weeping (בֹּכֶה) and casting himself down before the house of God … for the people wept a great weeping”.
“I sat down and wept and mourned days, and was fasting and praying before the God of heaven.”
“This day is holy to Yahweh your God; do not mourn nor weep”, for the people wept at hearing the words of the law.
“Between the porch and the altar let the priests, the ministers of Yahweh, weep, and say, Spare your people, Yahweh.”
“Should I weep in the fifth month, separating myself, as I have done these many years?”
“I wept with fasting of my soul.”
The congregation “weeping at the door of the tent of meeting”.
“The sons of Israel shall come, they and the sons of Judah together, going and weeping (הָלוֹךְ וּבָכוֹ) they shall go, and seek Yahweh their God.”

senses.definition: To weep at or upon someone (עַל, “in the ears of”) to press a demand or a grievance: Israel's weeping for flesh in the wilderness, Samson's wife weeping on him for the riddle.

evidence.note: “The mixed multitude lusted, and the sons of Israel also wept again, and said, Who will give us flesh to eat?”
Moses: “they weep on me (יִבְכּוּ עָלַי), saying, Give us flesh.”
“You have wept in the ears of Yahweh, saying, Who will give us flesh?”
“You have rejected Yahweh who is among you, and have wept before him, saying, Why did we come out of Egypt?”
After the spies' report “the people wept that night”.
“You returned and wept before Yahweh, but Yahweh did not listen to your voice.”
Samson's wife “wept on him (עָלָיו) and said, You only hate me”; she wept the seven days until he told her.

senses.definition: Twice, a participle of women mourning one taken away: Rachel weeping for her sons, and the women of Jerusalem weeping for the Tammuz at the gate of the house of Yahweh.

evidence.note: “A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation, bitter weeping (בְּכִי תַמְרוּרִים): Rachel weeping (מְבַכָּה) for her sons; she refuses to be comforted for her sons, because they are not (אֵינֶנּוּ).”
“There sat the women weeping for the Tammuz (מְבַכּוֹת אֶת־הַתַּמּוּז)”: a lament for a god counted dead, among the abominations of the house of Yahweh.
Quotes Jer 31:15 of the children of Bethlehem slain by Herod: “Rachel weeping for her children (Peshitta בָּכְיָא)”.

evidence.locator: Gen.21.16, וַתֵּבְךְּ → ἔκλαυσεν; Psa.126.6, וּבָכֹה → ἔκλαιον; Ecc.3.4, לִבְכּוֹת → κλαῦσαι; Ezr.10.1, בֹּכֶה → κλαίων; κλαίω renders בָּכָה ×70

“Blessed are you who weep (κλαίοντες) now, for you shall laugh”: the turn of Ecc 3:4 and Psa 126:6.
Jesus “saw the city and wept over it (ἔκλαυσεν ἐπ᾽ αὐτήν)”, as Jeremiah wept for the slain of his people (Jer 8:23).
“Do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.”
“Weep with those who weep.”
The kings and merchants of the earth weep over Babylon, as the seafarers over Tyre (Ezk 27:31).
The women “who bewailed and lamented him (ἐθρήνουν αὐτόν)”, to whom he said, “do not weep for me”.
“We lamented (ἐθρηνήσαμεν) to you, and you did not mourn.”

parallels.note: “Mourn, lament”: the funeral wailing that goes with weeping.
“Mourn”: Absalom's father, the people at the reading of the law, Nehemiah for Jerusalem.
“Fast”: weeping and fasting together, for the dead and before Yahweh.

opposites.note: “Laugh”: a time to weep and a time to laugh.
“Ringing cry of joy”: weeping at evening, joy in the morning; sowing in weeping, reaping with joy.
“Shout”: at the founding of the second house the shout of joy could not be told from the sound of weeping.

weep a great weeping, weep bitterly
fall on the neck of and weep
weep sorely (with the infinitive absolute); with a negative, weep no more

senses.definition: The act and the sound of weeping: a voice of weeping that others hear, weeping that marks the face, drink mingled with weeping.

evidence.note: Joseph “gave forth his voice in weeping (בִּבְכִי), and the Egyptians heard”.
“Yahweh has heard the voice of my weeping (קוֹל בִּכְיִי).”
“Weeping (בֶּכִי) may lodge at evening, but in the morning a ringing cry of joy.”
The people could not tell the sound of the shout of joy from “the sound of the weeping of the people”.
“I will rejoice in Jerusalem … and the voice of weeping (קוֹל בְּכִי) shall be heard in her no more, nor the voice of crying.”
“My face is red with weeping.”
“I have mingled my drink with weeping.”
“I will be bitter in weeping (בַּבֶּכִי); do not try to comfort me.”
“Bitter weeping (בְּכִי תַמְרוּרִים).”
“Keep your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears … they shall return from the land of the enemy.”
Over Moab: going up to the high places to weep, going up the ascent of Luhith with weeping.
“For the mountains I will take up weeping and wailing.”
“They wept a great weeping (בְּכִי גָדוֹל).”
The Peshitta's noun בֶּכְיָא in its quotation of Jer 31:15.

senses.definition: Weeping that goes with fasting, mourning and supplication, as the sign of turning back to Yahweh.

evidence.note: “Return to me with all your heart, with fasting and with weeping and with mourning.”
“A voice is heard on the bare heights, the weeping of the supplications of the sons of Israel, for they have perverted their way.”
“With weeping they shall come, and with supplications I will lead them … for I am a father to Israel.”
“Yahweh of armies called that day for weeping and mourning, baldness and girding with sackcloth.”
“Great mourning among the Jews, and fasting and weeping and wailing.”
“Covering the altar of Yahweh with tears, with weeping and groaning”, yet he no longer regards the offering.

senses.gloss: (the days of) weeping for the dead
senses.definition: In יְמֵי בְכִי, the set days of weeping for one dead.

evidence.note: “The days of weeping, the mourning for Moses (יְמֵי בְכִי אֵבֶל מֹשֶׁה), were ended.”

senses.definition: Of water: the “weeping” of streams, their trickling or seepage, which the miner binds up to lay the rock bare.

evidence.note: “He binds the streams from weeping (מִבְּכִי נְהָרוֹת), and the hidden thing he brings out to light.”

words.summary: Once, beside the verb, in Ezr 10:1.

senses.definition: Weeping, as the object of the verb: “they wept a great weeping”.

evidence.note: “The people wept much weeping (בָכוּ … הַרְבֵּה־בֶכֶה)” as Ezra prayed and confessed.

words.summary: Once: the seventy days of Egypt's weeping for Jacob (Gen 50:3).

senses.definition: The set time of weeping for one dead.

evidence.note: “When the days of his weeping (יְמֵי בְכִיתוֹ) were past, Joseph spoke to the house of Pharaoh”: the seventy days of Gen 50:3.

words.summary: Once, in the name of the oak below Bethel where Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, was buried.

senses.definition: Weeping for the dead, in the name given to the oak where Deborah was buried.

evidence.note: Deborah died and was buried below Bethel under the oak, “and he called its name אַלּוֹן בָּכוּת”.

words.gloss: baca tree (kind unknown); the valley of Baca
words.summary: Five times: trees near the valley of Rephaim (2Sa 5:23–24; 1Ch 14:14–15) and a dry valley on the pilgrims' road (Psa 84:7). Its tie to בכה “weep” is not shown: it may be a tree that drips (weeps) gum or sap, or, with Arabic bakaʾa “have little milk; (of a well) have its water sink”, a dry place; Psa 84:7 sets the valley against a spring. The kind of tree is not known from scripture.

senses.definition: Trees whose tops rustled with “the sound of marching” as Yahweh went out before David against the Philistines.

evidence.note: “Come upon them opposite the בְּכָאִים.”
“When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the בְּכָאִים, then act promptly, for then Yahweh has gone out before you.”

senses.definition: A valley through which those whose strength is in Yahweh pass on the way to Zion, making it a spring.

evidence.note: “Passing through the valley of Baca (בְּעֵמֶק הַבָּכָא) they make it a spring; the early rain also covers it with blessings.”

senses.definition: The Peshitta's word for weeping in the New Testament: weeping for the dead, for sin, over a city, and the weeping that is to be turned to laughter.

evidence.note: Quoting Jer 31:15: “Rachel weeping (בָּכְיָא) for her children.”
Peter “went out and wept bitterly”.
Jesus wept over Jerusalem.
“Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh”; and “woe to you who laugh now” (Luk 6:25).
“All were weeping and bewailing her; he said, Do not weep; she is not dead but sleeps.”
Mary going to the tomb “to weep there”.
Mary stood weeping outside the tomb.
“You shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice … your sorrow shall be turned into joy.”
“I tell you even weeping, they are the enemies of the cross of Christ.”
John wept much; “do not weep: the lion of the tribe of Judah … has prevailed”.
The kings of the earth weep over Babylon.

senses.definition: Weeping: Rachel's for her children, and the weeping and gnashing of teeth of those cast out of the kingdom at the coming of the Son of man.

evidence.note: Quoting Jer 31:15, “weeping and much wailing”.
“There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, and yourselves thrust out.”
“They all wept much (great weeping), and fell on Paul's neck and kissed him”, as Joseph on Benjamin's (Gen 45:14).

cognates.gloss: weep, shed tears, cry aloud in grief; weep for (the dead); (form IV) make weep; (of a cloud) rain
cognates.note: The same verb, with the same construction: bakā ʿalayhi “weep for him”, and the transitive bakāhu, weeping for the dead with mention of their good deeds. Lane's distinction of bukāʾ, the voice of weeping, and bukā, the shedding of tears, answers to the Hebrew's voice lifted up and eyes running with water. doctrine.statement: Scripture weeps for the dead as for those who are gone. Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her (Gen 23:2); Egypt wept for Jacob seventy days and Israel for Moses thirty (Gen 50:3; Deu 34:8). Jacob would go down mourning to his son “to the grave” (Gen 37:35). David fasted and wept while his child lived, in hope that Yahweh would be gracious; when the child died he stopped, saying, “Can I bring him back again? I go to him, but he will not return to me” (2Sa 12:21–23). Jeremiah says, “weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall return no more” (Jer 22:10). Rachel weeps for her sons “because they are not” (Jer 31:15), and Matthew sets the slaughter of the children of Bethlehem under that verse (Mat 2:18). Yahweh's comfort to her is not that her sons live on somewhere, but “refrain your voice from weeping … they shall return from the land of the enemy … your sons shall return to their own border” (Jer 31:16–17). The New Testament names death that enemy, the last to be destroyed, when those who are Christ's are made alive at his coming (1Co 15:22–26). Jesus told the mourners of Jairus' daughter, “do not weep; she is not dead but sleeps”, and raised her (Luk 8:52–55). From the verses: the dead are not; weeping for them is right; and the hope that ends the weeping is their return from death by resurrection.

The prophets place the end of weeping in a place and a people: “a people shall dwell in Zion at Jerusalem; you shall weep no more” (Isa 30:19), and “I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people, and the voice of weeping shall be heard in her no more” (Isa 65:19; compare Isa 25:8; Rev 21:4). The way there begins in weeping: “with weeping they shall come, and with supplications I will lead them” (Jer 31:9); “the sons of Israel and the sons of Judah together, going and weeping … shall seek Yahweh their God; they shall ask the way to Zion” (Jer 50:4–5). Those who sow in tears reap with a ringing cry (Psa 126:5–6), and Jesus says, “blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luk 6:21). He also names a weeping that remains: “there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, and yourselves thrust out; and they shall come from east and west … and sit down in the kingdom of God” (Luk 13:28–29; Mat 8:11–12), said of the time the Son of man comes and the servants give account (Mat 24:50–51; 25:19, 30–31). From the verses: the kingdom in which weeping ends is set in Jerusalem and the land, with Israel gathered and the fathers and prophets present in it; the weeping of the rejected belongs to that day, when they see it and are shut out of it.

note: Drafted 2026-11-19. Root key בכה. BDB keys assigned: b.bq.aa verb, b.bq.ac בְּכִי, b.bq.ab בֶּכֶה, b.bq.ae בְּכִית, b.bq.ad בָּכוּת, and b.bp.cc בָּכָא (filed in the database under בית by alphabet; bayit.json's note left it out as belonging to בכא/בכה), given its own root key בכא. LEFT OUT: b.bq.af בֹּכִים Bochim (Jdg 2:1, 5), a place name: places get no name entry, and its naming is cited under weep-before-yahweh (Jdg 2:4–5). No personal names are formed from the root (TIPNR has only the places Bochim and Allon-bacuth). SHARED TOKENS: the brief's ten verb tokens with no stem are בְּכִי and Bochim; b.bq.af's two “qal” tokens (Job 30:31; Ezr 3:12) are the verb's participle בֹּכִים. בָּכוּת occurs only in the place name אַלּוֹן בָּכוּת (Gen 35:8) and is kept as a noun. No Biblical Aramaic word (Daniel and Ezra have none); the Peshitta's words are SEDRA root 272 בכא, lexemes 390 (verb), 391 בכיא, 392 בכתא (Act 20:37 only); its verb is entered as peal throughout, which the SEDRA forms suggest but were not checked form by form. Lemma pointings בֶּכְיָא, בְּכָתָא follow SEDRA's vocalised forms. Greek: no loans. The Septuagint renders בָּכָא at 2Sa 5:24 and Psa 84:7 by κλαυθμών “place of weeping”, a translator's reading and no evidence. Ge'ez: Dillmann's column (521–522) was found from the archive scan's OCR (page n284) between legible column heads 519–520 and 525–526; confirm on the scan. LEADS NOT FOLLOWED: Ugaritic bkyt “female mourner” (Wiktionary; DULAT not consulted); CAD for bakû; Payne Smith for the Syriac beyond SEDRA; Old and Imperial Aramaic (CAL); Arabic بكأ for בָּכָא is a guess. Klein's Arabic baka'a “it dripped” (for the balsam's resin) was not found in Lane, whose بكأ has only “have little milk/water”. OPEN QUESTIONS: (1) whether בָּכָא belongs to this root at all, and what tree it is; (2) whether Job 28:11 מִבְּכִי is the noun “weeping” used of trickling water (taken so here) or another word; (3) the two doctrine statements are reasoned conclusions for review, especially the reading of the weeping and gnashing of teeth.
